records.title: Dangun and the Founding of Gojoseon
records.summary: Recorded in the 13th-century Samguk Yusa, Hwanung, the son of the Lord of Heaven, descended to Mount Taebaek to govern humanity with three thousand heavenly spirits. A bear and a tiger approached him, pleading to be transformed into human beings. Hwanung gave them a bundle of sacred mugwort and twenty cloves of garlic, instructing them to remain inside a dark cave for one hundred days without seeing sunlight. The impatient tiger abandoned the trial after twenty days, but the steadfast bear endured the penance, emerging on the twenty-first day as a beautiful woman named Ungnyeo. Hwanung married her, and she gave birth to Dangun Wanggeom, who founded Gojoseon—the first Korean kingdom—in 2333 BCE at Pyongyang.
records.historical_period: Ancient Gojoseon origin (recorded 1281 CE by monk Iryeon in Samguk Yusa)
records.region_or_community: Mount Taebaek and Pyongyang, Korean Peninsula

records.title: The Tale of Chunhyang (Chunhyangjeon)
records.summary: A masterwork of Korean pansori oral narrative, Sung Chunhyang, the brilliant daughter of a retired kisaeng courtesan in Namwon, falls deeply in love with noble scholar Lee Mongryong. The lovers exchange secret marriage vows before Mongryong must depart for Hanyang (Seoul) to sit the civil service examinations. A tyrannical, corrupt new magistrate, Byeon Hakdo, demands that Chunhyang become his concubine; steadfast in marital fidelity, she refuses and is subjected to brutal torture, starvation, and imprisoned in the dungeon. Returning secretly as a royal secret inspector (Amhaeng-eosa) disguised as a ragged beggar, Mongryong storms the magistrate's banquet with his badge of office, arresting the tyrant and vindicating Chunhyang's unwavering virtue.
records.historical_period: Joseon Dynasty (popularized in 18th-century Pansori oral theater)

records.title: The Sun and the Moon: Brother and Sister and the Tiger
records.summary: While returning home over mountain passes with rice cakes for her children, a poor widow is ambushed by a ferocious tiger that demands: 'Give me a rice cake and I won't eat you!' After consuming all her cakes, the beast devours the mother, dresses in her clothes, and arrives at her cottage to trick her young son, Haesik, and daughter, Dalsik. Realizing the deception from the hairy paws, the clever children scramble up a tall zelkova tree and climb onto the roof. Cornered, they pray to Heaven for a rope; a sturdy golden rope descends and pulls them into the sky, where the boy becomes the Sun and the shy girl becomes the Moon. The pursuing tiger receives a rotten straw rope from heaven, falling into a sorghum field to be impaled, its blood staining the stalks red.
alternate_names: The Brother and Sister Who Became Sun and Moon
records.historical_period: Traditional Joseon Era oral nursery lore
records.region_or_community: Rural mountain villages throughout the Korean Peninsula

records.title: The Gumiho of Mount Jiri (Nine-Tailed Fox)
records.summary: In Korean supernatural folklore, a gumiho is a fox spirit that lives for one thousand years, growing nine tails and mastering dark sorcery to transform into an irresistible, alluring maiden. Dwelling in the rugged gorges of Mount Jiri, the creature preys on solitary travelers, consuming human hearts and livers to sustain her life-force. Unlike Chinese or Japanese fox spirits, the Korean gumiho yearns deeply to become genuinely mortal human: if she lives with a human husband for one hundred days without him ever discovering her secret or speaking of her true identity, the curse is broken and she becomes a true human. Tragic betrayals on the ninety-ninth night often force her to return to the wilderness in tears.
records.historical_period: Three Kingdoms to Joseon Dynasty oral folklore
records.region_or_community: Jirisan Mountain National Park, South Gyeongsang and Jeolla

records.title: The Filial Daughter Shim Cheong
records.summary: Raised by her blind father Shim Hakgyu after her mother's death, Shim Cheong is the paragon of filial piety (hyo). When a deceitful Buddhist monk claims that an offering of three hundred sacks of polished rice to the temple will restore her father's eyesight, the impoverished maiden sells herself to merchant sailors as a human sacrifice to appease the Dragon King of the turbulent Indangsu Sea. Leaping fearlessly into the roaring waves, the Dragon King is so moved by her supreme devotion that he preserves her inside a colossal lotus blossom floating on the waters. Rescued by the Emperor, who marries her, she hosts a grand royal banquet for all blind citizens of the realm, where her joyful reunion causes her weeping father's eyes to open miraculously.
records.historical_period: Joseon Dynasty (popularized in 18th-century Pansori oral cycles)
records.region_or_community: Indangsu sea crossing near Baengnyeong Island and Hwanghae

records.title: Heungbu and Nolbu: The Swallow's Magic Gourd
records.summary: In this foundational Korean moral fable, two brothers live in stark contrast: elder brother Nolbu is a wealthy, cruel miser who expels younger brother Heungbu and his large family into poverty during winter. In his ramshackle hut, Heungbu rescues a baby swallow whose leg was broken by a snake, carefully splinting the bone with silk thread. In spring, the swallow returns from the south with a magical pumpkin seed. Planting the seed, Heungbu harvests colossal gourds; sawing them open, they spill out treasures of gold, silks, and palace builders. Envious Nolbu intentionally catches a healthy swallow, snaps its leg, and splints it to get a seed. When Nolbu saws his gourds, terrifying goblin demons (dokkaebi), debt collectors, and mud floods burst out, stripping him of all his wealth.
alternate_names: The Two Brothers and the Swallow
records.historical_period: Late Joseon Era (popularized c. 18th Century in Pansori Heungbuga)
records.region_or_community: Jeolla and Chungcheong rural agricultural heartland

records.title: The Woodcutter and the Heavenly Maiden
records.summary: A kind, impoverished mountain woodcutter rescues a hunted deer from a hunter's arrow in the Diamond Mountains (Geumgangsan). In gratitude, the deer informs him that heavenly celestial maidens descend from the sky to bathe in a secluded mountain pond on midsummer night, advising him to hide one pair of winged robes (nalgaeot) so the maiden cannot return to the heavens until she has borne three children. The woodcutter marries the maiden and they raise two children in happiness. Overcome with pity when his wife weeps for her heavenly parents, the woodcutter returns the robe prematurely. Putting on the robes, she gathers both children under her arms and ascends back to the heavens, leaving the weeping woodcutter with a magical bucket to follow her.
alternate_names: The Heavenly Maiden of Mount Geumgang

records.title: Hong Gildong: The Righteous Outlaw
records.summary: Born to a high minister and a concubine maid during the Joseon Dynasty, Hong Gildong is a prodigy in martial arts, Taoist magic, and military strategy, yet forbidden by strict neo-Confucian caste laws (seoeol) from calling his father 'Father' or his brother 'Brother.' Surviving an assassination attempt orchestrated by his father's jealous concubine, Gildong flees into the mountains and becomes leader of the Hwalbindang ('League of Those Who Save the Impoverished'). Robbing corrupt magistrates and distributing wealth to starving peasants, Gildong uses Taoist straw effigies to create phantom duplicates of himself in eight provinces simultaneously, before sailing west to found the utopian island kingdom of Yuldo.
records.historical_period: Mid-Joseon Era (written c. early 17th Century by Heo Gyun)
records.region_or_community: Hanyang (Seoul) and Gangwon / Jeolla mountain hideouts

records.title: The Magic Mirror and the Dragon of the East Sea
records.summary: A dutiful fisherman from the eastern coast of Gangwon rescues a golden carp from a beach puddle following a violent storm, gently returning it to the open sea. That night, an envoy from the Dragon Palace of the East Sea (Yonggung) escorts the fisherman beneath the waves to the coral court of the Dragon King, who reveals the carp was his youngest prince. In gratitude, the Dragon King presents the fisherman with a miraculous bronze mirror that reveals any hidden treasure or impending maritime storm when polished. Returning to his coastal hamlet, the fisherman uses the mirror to save his village fleet from typhoons and unearth forgotten buried granaries to feed his neighbors.
records.historical_period: Traditional Maritime Folklore of the East Sea
records.region_or_community: Sokcho and Gangneung coastal fishing ports, Gangwon Province

records.title: The Toad Bridegroom and the Golden Water
records.summary: An impoverished elderly woman gives birth to a large speaking toad, rearing it with affectionate care. Reaching adulthood, the toad insists on proposing marriage to the youngest daughter of the wealthy village magistrate. While the two elder haughty daughters recoil in disgust, the gentle youngest daughter agrees out of compassion. On the wedding night, the toad asks his bride to slit open his rough amphibian skin with scissors; stepping out from the shed pelt, he transforms into a radiant, noble prince from the heavenly realms who was temporarily exiled to earth for a celestial offense, rewarding his faithful bride with prosperity and honor.
